title: Ten Spreadsheets That Make a Startup Easier to Run
summary: Ten Spreadsheets That Make a Startup Easier to Run
body_markdown:
The most useful spreadsheet at a startup usually has a question at the top. Can we make payroll in March? What happens if a renewal slips? How many months does this round buy? Those questions lead to better models than “let’s build a financial model.” The model gets smaller, and you find out sooner which number you actually need.


Start with what you can verify: unrestricted cash in the bank, invoices with payment dates, and the next payroll. Use assumptions for the rest, but put them in visible cells. These ten sheets each answer a question. You can do the first one this afternoon.


## Know where the cash goes


1. **Monthly burn and runway.** Use recent net operating cash outflow to estimate how long unrestricted cash lasts. Keep funding proceeds and unusual items visible separately. If monthly receipts are $45,000 and operating payouts are $75,000, net burn is $30,000. At that pace, $360,000 lasts about 12 months. That is a quick estimate, not a forecast.[Stripe’s runway guide](https://stripe.com/resources/more/how-to-calculate-startup-runway) covers the basic calculation.
2. **13-week cash plan.** Put receipts, payroll, tax and vendor payments in the week they move cash. Roll each closing cash balance into the next week’s opening balance. This picks up the problem a monthly runway number can hide: a big invoice due in week eight does nothing for payroll in week six.
3. **Receivables tracker.** Track each invoice's balance, due date, and expected collection date. A prediction belongs in the expected column; a payment belongs in actuals. Separating them forces you to notice when an old assumption is still holding up your forecast.
4. **Hiring plan.** Enter start month, salary, employer costs and one-time setup separately. Compare steady monthly cost with actual cash in the first quarter. A hire who starts in June won’t have 12 months of salary in this year’s budget, but will have 12 in next year’s.


## Find out what the business can repeat


1. **MRR bridge.** Start with opening monthly recurring revenue, then add new and expansion MRR and subtract contraction and churn. Show reactivations separately. Reconcile to billing and keep one-time fees out. The closing total says how big the recurring business is; the components say how it got there.
2. **Retention by cohort.** Group customers by when they started and divide their current recurring revenue by the same group’s starting recurring revenue. Hold membership fixed. Show logo retention next to revenue retention so expansion from a few accounts doesn’t hide how many left.
3. **Gross margin and payback.** Subtract direct costs to serve from recurring revenue to get gross profit. Compare acquisition cost with monthly gross profit per new customer for a rough payback period. Match dates and cohorts, and leave payback undefined if gross profit isn’t positive.
4. **Base and downside cash cases.** Give each scenario its own receipts and outflows and look for the first month cash falls below your reserve. Stress one driver you can respond to, such as collections lag or a slower hiring date. Changing growth, pricing and expense together may produce a wide range without showing what to do.


## Decide what to sell and when


1. **SAFE dilution and ownership.** Track each instrument instead of treating them all as the same. For a simple post-money cap SAFE where the cap controls, investment divided by the cap illustrates ownership sold before the priced financing. Don’t plug a discount-only, MFN or pre-money SAFE into that shortcut.[YC’s SAFE guide and forms](https://www.ycombinator.com/safe) explain the structure. Use signed terms and a proper capitalization model for a financing decision.
2. **Raise size and milestones.** Start with the date by which you expect to prove something, such as getting a second customer cohort to renew. Calculate net cash needed through that date, add your reserve, and subtract unrestricted cash already on hand. A financing target is easier to evaluate when you can say what evidence the capital buys.


Try the cash plan before building all ten. Compare it with your bank balance next Friday. If the forecast was wrong, label the cause rather than smoothing the result. After a month of this, you'll know which numbers you can safely put in the rest of the workbook.
